en: Some power lines carry electricity across a whole country.
Why such crazy high voltage?
And why do the longest ones use direct current, not the alternating current in your wall?
Take a guess.
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
Let's follow the power.
A power plant has a fixed amount of power to send.
Power equals voltage times current.
So it's lots of current at low voltage, or a little current at high voltage.
But every wire has resistance, so current makes it hot.
The heat you lose grows with the current squared.
Double the current, and you waste four times the heat.
So engineers crank up the voltage.
Same power, less current, far less heat.
Transformers step it back down near the city.
But your wall gives you alternating current.
It flips direction fifty or sixty times every second.
On a very long line, that flipping keeps filling and emptying the line, like a giant battery.
That extra current crowds the wires but does no useful work.
And every AC grid on the line must swing in perfect step, like dancers.
Across thousands of kilometers that gets wobbly, and one fault can spread into a blackout.
Direct current fixes this.
It flows one way, so nothing flips and nobody keeps step.
A government energy lab says it can cut losses by up to fifty percent.
The catch?
Both ends need giant converter stations to turn AC into DC and back.
They can eat up to sixty percent of the cost.
So for shorter trips, AC wins.
For huge power over more than about five hundred kilometers, high voltage DC wins.
Stay curious!
